headline: Composting returns nutrients to the earth—death feeds new life in an endless cycle
universal_truth: Nothing is truly wasted in closed loops; what one process discards, another needs
fun_facts: Compost contains billions of microorganisms per gram that break down organic matter
About 30% of household waste could be composted instead of landfilled
Finished compost is so nutrient-rich it's called 'black gold' by gardeners
discussion_questions: What 'waste' in your life could nourish something new?
How do you close loops rather than create dead ends?
What cycles are you part of that you don't usually notice?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: Apple cores become soil that grows apple trees. Death feeds life feeds death feeds life. Composting isn't just rot—it's transformation. What one organism discards, another organism needs. The cycle never stops.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Composting seems like decay, but it's really cycling. What does nature's closed-loop system teach us?

options.text: Waste is a design flaw—in natural systems, every output becomes an input somewhere else; true efficiency creates closed loops where nothing is truly discarded
options.response: Yes. Nature has no garbage—everything cycles. What we call 'waste' is just resources in the wrong place. Design for loops, not lines.
It is decomposition, but the key insight is that decomposition feeds composition...

q1.title: Closed Loops
q1.script: In nature, there's no 'away' to throw things. Everything cycles. Leaves fall, decompose, become soil, feed trees, become leaves. Designing for closed loops eliminates waste entirely.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Closed Loops"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Transformation Agents
q2.script: Composting requires decomposers—bacteria, fungi, worms. They do the work of transformation. Every cycle needs agents who break down the old to feed the new.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Personal Composting
q3.script: You can compost experiences too—letting failures decompose into lessons, disappointments into wisdom, endings into new beginnings. Nothing is wasted if you close the loop.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Nothing is truly wasted in closed loops. What one process discards, another needs. Design for cycles, not dead ends.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 282. Tomorrow, we'll explore deciding what you want—goal setting. Until then, consider how you might close loops in your life.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Loop Closure - What Waste Could Become Input?
growTrack.learning_objective: Identify opportunities to close loops and eliminate waste
growTrack.activity: What do you discard that could become input elsewhere? Failed projects contain lessons. Ended relationships contain wisdom. Old skills have new applications. How can you compost your 'waste' into nutrients for new growth?
